title: Choral evensong
hookLine: a sung service at dusk, with the Magnificat and Nunc Dimittis
last: PRAYER HANGS ON MORNING AND EVENING.

cards: The light is going outside a stone chapel. A few people sit in the carved wooden stalls: a student with a backpack, someone still in work clothes, a visitor who wandered in out of the cold.
A bell, an organ note, and the choir begins. You can sing along if you know it, or just sit.

The choir carries most of the singing: the psalm for the day, a song after each of the two readings, prayers sung back and forth, and then out into the dark. It's yesterday's Evening Prayer, set to music.

teach.b: The two songs at the center of evensong come from the first pages of Luke, and they belong to two people at opposite ends of a story. You've met both before on this path. The first is Mary's.
She has just been told she will bear a child, and visits her cousin Elizabeth. There she says: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour."

Listen to where it goes: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Not a lullaby.
A world turned over. In church it's known by its first word in Latin, Magnificat. The second song is Simeon's.
Luke says it had been shown to him that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord's Christ.

teach.h: SIMEON: NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT.
teach.b: When Mary and Joseph bring the baby into the temple, Simeon takes him in his arms and blesses God: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation."
Its Latin name is its first words, Nunc dimittis: now you let go.

teach.h: A BEGINNING AND AN ENDING AT DUSK.
teach.b: So evensong sets a beginning and an ending side by side: a woman carrying a child, singing about the low lifted up, and a man who has waited, ready to go in peace.
Sung at dusk, Simeon's words can be heard as a word about the day itself. And these songs aren't only Anglican. Catholic evening prayer, Vespers, sings the Magnificat too.

how: Choral evensong is sung by choirs in Anglican cathedrals, college chapels and some parish churches, usually in the late afternoon; people may join in the responses or simply sit and listen.

o: a lullaby hymn sung to children at bedtime on Sundays

games.q: the songs of evensong — tap the pairs.

s: at evensong the congregation has to sing everything
the choir carries most of it. you can join in, or simply sit and listen.
both of evensong's songs come from Luke's Gospel
Mary's song is in Luke 1, Simeon's in Luke 2.
the Magnificat is a gentle song with no edge to it
"He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree."

games.q: you're Simeon in the temple, waiting, as Luke says, for the consolation of Israel. a couple walks in with their baby. what do you do?
o: ask the priests to bless the child.
take him in your arms and bless God.
slip out and tell your friends.
games.why: he takes the child up in his arms, blesses God, and says, "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace."

practice: If you can, play a recording of evensong, or just Simeon's song; if not, let one line come back by itself: now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace. Then let the day go, piece by piece: the meeting, the drive, the dishes.
Listening can be the whole prayer, and if you pray, hand the day back to God in Simeon's words.

wordCard.voice: Evensong. Evening Prayer sung at dusk, with Mary's Magnificat and Simeon's Nunc dimittis at its heart.

orig.note: Latin: (my soul) magnifies — the first word of Mary's song in Latin, and its name.

carryVoice: Your line: the day ends in song. Mary's song lifts the low; Simeon's lets go in peace. Good night.
